articles.title: The Preliminary Lunar Science Report for Artemis II is Out!
articles.description: Through photographs, spoken observations, drawings, and annotations, the Artemis II crew created a unique scientific record—one that is now available to the science community and the public for further study. Explore highlights here, and find the full suite of reports and select data resources at the bottom of the page.
articles.summary: The Artemis II mission crew has completed a comprehensive lunar science report documenting their observations and discoveries on the Moon. This rich scientific record advances our knowledge of lunar geology and prepares humanity for future lunar exploration.

articles.title: Discovery marks the first detection of variable water clouds outside of the solar system
articles.description: A Jupiter-sized world just 7.5 light-years away is cloudy, chemically complex and, it turns out, more like home than anyone expected. Using the James Webb Space Telescope, Brittany Miles, assistant astronomer at the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory, led a team that spent 11 hours staring at WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, collecting a spectrum of its light every 15 minutes.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers detect the first variable water clouds outside our solar system on a Jupiter-sized world just 7.5 light-years away. This discovery reveals an exoplanet with Earth-like atmospheric features, expanding our understanding of worlds beyond our system.

articles.title: Astronomers pinpoint the most distant fast radio burst ever detected
articles.description: Astronomers have detected and traced the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded, a powerful flash of radio waves that traveled for more than 10 billion years across the cosmos before reaching Earth.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers detect and trace the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded, providing insights into powerful cosmic events across the universe. This breakthrough expands our ability to study the deep cosmos.

articles.title: Francis Halzen Wins Nobel Physics Prize For Antarctic 'Ghost Particle' Hunt
articles.description: University of Wisconsin-Madison physicist Francis Halzen has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to understanding astrophysical neutrinos. Halzen led the development of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory beneath the Antarctic ice,…
articles.summary: Physicist Francis Halzen wins the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his groundbreaking work on the IceCube Antarctic observatory, which detects cosmic high-energy neutrinos from the universe's most extreme events.

articles.title: Francis Halzen Wins the Physics Nobel for an Antarctic Ice Observatory That Caught Cosmic High-Energy Neutrino
articles.description: Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his decisive contributions to IceCube, the Antarctic observatory that revealed high-energy neutrinos from cosmic sources.
articles.summary: Francis Halzen receives the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his decisive contributions to IceCube, the Antarctic ice observatory that revolutionized detection of cosmic high-energy neutrinos.

articles.title: Solar Orbiter tracks origin of mysterious magnetic switchbacks
articles.description: The European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has flown through an S-shaped kink known as a ‘switchback’ in the solar wind’s magnetic field. By fingerprinting the elusive particles within the switchback, Solar Orbiter has traced its origin back to the Sun’s surface and revealed more about solar magnetism – the unruly instigator of dangerous solar storms.
articles.summary: Solar Orbiter has successfully tracked the origin of mysterious magnetic switchbacks in the solar wind, advancing our understanding of solar dynamics. This discovery helps scientists decode the complex magnetic structures flowing from the Sun.

articles.title: Webb captures commotion from nebula’s stellar jets
articles.description:
Image:
			Webb captures commotion from nebula’s stellar jets
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has captured stunning imagery of energetic stellar jets erupting from a nebula in vivid detail. These observations reveal the dynamic processes of star formation in unprecedented clarity.

articles.title: Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors
articles.description:
Image:
			
This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us.
MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.
The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing, in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity.
The gravitationally lensed areas show multiple images of galaxies from when the Universe was young: a group of galaxies 2 billion years after the Big Bang, and a single galaxy just 800 million years old after the Big Bang. The galaxy group appears to be going through a merger, resulting in an enormous burst of star formation.
Astronomers have also identified individual bright ‘knots’ within the gravitationally lensed areas, corresponding to regions as small as 5 light-years across. These tiny clumps appear magnified by a factor of more than 300, in some cases.
A NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image of this same cluster was released in 2014. Take a moment to compare the two images; the difference between them is dramatic. The new Webb image reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier image. These galaxies were there all along, but Webb is much more sensitive to their much redder light.
The data behind this image come from two observing programmes (#5058, PI: Furtak; #6882, PI: Fujimoto) that leverage the ability of massive galaxy clusters to bring distant objects into view.
[Image Description: A massive galaxy cluster, made of many golden elliptical galaxies with the largest, brightest one in the centre. Heavily distorted orange galaxies appear all around the cluster, the largest concentrated in a large arc around the cluster's centre; these are images of very distant galaxies, created by gravitational lensing. A few galaxies are large and bluish-white in colour; bright, nearby stars are the same colour.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope reveals intricate galactic details through gravitational lensing acting as a cosmic magnifying glass. This Picture of the Month showcases the universe's most distant and ancient structures in remarkable detail.

articles.title: Astronomers Detect Potential ‘Second Generation’ Planet Around Dying Stellar White Dwarf
articles.description: Potential ‘Second generation’ planet detection around a dying stellar white dwarf opens a whole new chapter of exoplanetary science.
articles.summary: Astronomers have detected a potential planet orbiting a white dwarf, representing a remarkable discovery of second-generation planetary systems around stellar remnants. This finding expands the horizons of exoplanet science and stellar evolution.

articles.title: The Most Distant FRB Tells The Story Of Its Origin
articles.description: Astronomers use the Webb to study a distant fast radio burst and reveal clues as to the origin of these mysterious events.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has analyzed the most distant fast radio burst yet observed, revealing clues about the origin of these enigmatic cosmic signals. This breakthrough deepens our understanding of mysterious high-energy phenomena in the universe.

articles.title: A Student Finds Three Galaxies and Possibly Solves a Mystery
articles.description: It's not too often that a high school student-turned undergraduate gets three galaxies named after him, especially ones that are breaking the rules of star formation. Julian Shapiro, an astrophysics student at the University of California, Berkeley, found strange dwarf galaxies in the vicinity of the large spiral M101 while doing research into their star formation rates as a high school student. They're now known as Shapiro I, II, and III. In the process, he's become an inspiration to other students who might be interested in astrophysical research.
articles.summary: A high school student-turned-undergraduate has discovered three galaxies and potentially solved an astronomical mystery in the process. This achievement highlights the contributions young scientists can make to our understanding of the cosmos.

articles.title: Webb Observes "Extreme Debris Disks," Providing a Window into the Early Solar System
articles.description: In the early history of our solar system, scientists theorize that a Mars-sized object called Theia smashed into the infant Earth, creating the Earth-Moon system. Using Webb, astronomers are studying young star systems to learn more about the early Solar System's evolution.
articles.summary: Webb Space Telescope observations of extreme debris disks provide a window into our early solar system and the planetary formation processes that created it. These findings illuminate the dramatic collisions and dynamics that shaped our cosmic neighborhood.

articles.title: To Win A Nobel Prize, Go To The Ends Of The Earth
articles.description: Neutrinos are persnickety particles. We couldn't really detect neutrinos from deep space until Francis Halzen had a brilliant, Nobel Prize-winning idea.
articles.summary: Pioneering neutrino detection research conducted at Earth's remote locations has led to Nobel Prize recognition for breakthrough discoveries in particle physics. This achievement demonstrates how ambitious scientific endeavors at extreme locations unlock cosmic mysteries.

articles.title: NASA Selects GIMLI to Search the Marius Lunar Pit for a Potential Lunar Base Site
articles.description: NASA has selected a Planetary Science Institute-led proposal to investigate whether a potentially large underground cave extends beyond the opening of a lunar pit.
articles.summary: NASA selects GIMLI mission to investigate a potentially large underground cave in the Marius lunar pit as a candidate for a future lunar base site. This groundbreaking exploration could identify natural shelters for human habitation on the Moon.

articles.title: NASA advances LISA mission contributions with new test telescope
articles.description: NASA has taken the next step in the process of developing a new all-glass telescope for the LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) mission, a space observatory designed to detect ripples in space-time called gravitational waves.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: NASA advances the LISA mission by developing a new all-glass telescope for gravitational wave detection. This technological breakthrough represents a major step toward observing the universe through gravitational waves.

articles.title: Strong magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to grow beyond the Chandrasekhar limit
articles.description: When a dying star runs out of fuel and sheds its outer layers, its remaining core can become an approximately Earth-sized, extremely dense stellar remnant called a white dwarf. For a white dwarf that is not strongly rotating or magnetized, there is a well-known upper mass limit of about 1.4 times the mass of the sun, known as the Chandrasekhar limit.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Research demonstrates that strong magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to exceed the Chandrasekhar limit, challenging existing theories of stellar evolution. This finding opens new possibilities for understanding stellar remnants.

articles.title: SPHEREx spots menagerie of brown dwarfs with atmospheric water and methane
articles.description: NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the universe, Epoch of Reionization, and ices Explorer) space telescope is shedding light on brown dwarfs, celestial objects that blur the line between stars and exoplanets. New findings published in The Astrophysical Journal show that these dark and cloudy worlds have chemically rich atmospheres not unlike the giant planets in our own solar system.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: NASA's SPHEREx space telescope discovers a diverse population of brown dwarfs with atmospheric water and methane. These findings enhance our understanding of substellar objects throughout the galaxy.

articles.title: Largest 2D map of the universe helps scientists discover new gravitational lenses
articles.description: Using data from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, with help from artificial intelligence, an international team of scientists has discovered 70 new gravitational lenses—rare cosmic alignments that act as natural magnifying glasses. The new lenses further expand one of the largest collections of confirmed lenses to date and will allow scientists to study dark matter, galaxy evolution and the structure of the universe.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: An international team uses DESI Legacy Imaging Survey data and artificial intelligence to create the largest 2D map of the universe and discover new gravitational lenses. This achievement enhances our ability to study dark matter and cosmic structure.

articles.title: NASA is searching for hidden caves to build its first Moon base
articles.description: NASA is preparing for humanity’s first Moon base with three investigations that will hunt for underground shelters, uncover hidden ice, and track dangerous conditions on the lunar surface. The findings could reveal how astronauts can survive and thrive on the Moon while laying the groundwork for future journeys to Mars.
articles.summary: NASA launches three investigations to search for underground caves and shelters on the Moon to support humanity's first lunar base. This strategic approach combines exploration and innovation to enable long-term lunar habitation.

articles.title: MIT astronomers catch a star in a feast that could last billions of years
articles.description: Astronomers have discovered a bizarre star system about 300 light-years from Earth where a small star is slowly devouring a nearby brown dwarf, an object too massive to be a planet but too small to be a true star. Unlike stars that rapidly swallow their companions, this one is gradually stealing material in a process that could continue for billions of years.
articles.summary: MIT astronomers discover a remarkable binary star system 300 light-years away where a small star is slowly being consumed in a cosmic feast lasting potentially billions of years. This rare system provides unique insights into stellar dynamics and evolution.

articles.title: NASA’s Webb finds signs of Mars-sized worlds smashing together
articles.description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope is giving astronomers a glimpse of the kinds of violent collisions that may have shaped our own solar system, including the giant impact thought to have created the Moon. By studying 21 rare “extreme debris disks” around young stars, researchers found that their dust can reveal the scale and intensity of planetary collisions.
articles.summary: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observes evidence of Mars-sized planetary collisions in a distant star system. These observations reveal the violent formation processes that shape planetary systems across the universe.

articles.title: Hubble Space Telescope may have found a planet born after its star died
articles.description: A strange chemical signature in old Hubble observations may point to a planet that formed after its star had already died. Astronomers found unusually high levels of niobium around the white dwarf HS 0209+0832, suggesting some of the star’s expelled material may have assembled into a new gas giant. TESS data also hints at a Jupiter-sized planet orbiting just 3.7 million miles from the star.
articles.summary: Hubble Space Telescope observations reveal a mysterious chemical signature suggesting a planet may have formed after its star's death, challenging our understanding of planetary formation.

articles.title: A 9-billion-year-old signal could help explain dark energy
articles.description: A Canadian radio telescope has detected the faint glow of hydrogen from billions of years ago using only its own observations, proving a long-awaited way to map the distant universe can actually work. CHIME can use this hydrogen signal to trace how matter is spread across space and measure how the universe has expanded over time, offering a powerful new way to investigate dark energy.
articles.summary: A Canadian radio telescope has detected ancient hydrogen signals from 9 billion years ago, offering new insights into dark energy and the universe's expansion history.

articles.title: Researchers May Have Directly Glimpsed an Exoplanet’s Magnetic Field for the First Time, Building Hope of Peering Deeper Into Faraway Worlds
articles.description: Radio signals emanating from Beta Pictoris b suggest that this young and massive exoplanet has a strong magnetic field and intense auroral show
articles.summary: Radio signals from exoplanet Beta Pictoris b suggest it possesses a strong magnetic field, marking the first direct glimpse of an exoplanet's magnetosphere and opening new avenues for studying distant worlds.

articles.title: Nasa struggled to sample Bennu until Brian May revealed its hidden dangers
articles.description: A rock musician working at a computer might seem an unlikely figure in an asteroid-sampling mission, but Brian May brought a specialist skill to Nasa’s
articles.summary: Brian May, the legendary Queen guitarist and astrophysicist, contributed crucial insights that helped NASA successfully sample asteroid Bennu by identifying previously unknown hazards. His unique combination of musical talent and scientific expertise proved invaluable to one of NASA's most ambitious sample-return missions.

articles.title: Weekly Spaceflight News - Rocket Lab Secures 20 New Launches [6:16]
articles.description: In this week's industry update, SpaceX's Falcon program joined in on the action for a huge week for the company with several marquee missions. Elsewhere, Blue Origin is making progress towards not just returning to flight, but also towards a greater New Glenn…
articles.summary: Rocket Lab secured 20 new launch contracts while SpaceX's Falcon program achieved a landmark week for the commercial spaceflight industry. This represents major momentum in the private space launch sector.

articles.title: World Space Week 2026: The rocket revolution is happening above us — How cheaper launches could change everyday life on Earth
articles.description: Sixty-nine years after Sputnik's launch marked the beginning of the Space Age, new advancements are reshaping space access. Reusable rockets, such as SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Starship, are cost-effective alternatives to traditional expendable launch vehicles. Th…
articles.summary: World Space Week 2026 celebrates how the rocket revolution and cheaper launch costs are transforming space access and enabling practical benefits for life on Earth. Advances in reusable rocket technology promise to reshape humanity's relationship with space.

articles.title: Mars’s oddest cloud may be even odder than we thought
articles.description: Scientists using the European Space Agency's Mars Express, in combination with a state-of-the-art meteorological model of the Red Planet, have found that there may be some very exotic physics behind Mars’s most curious cloud.
articles.summary: Mars Express data reveals that one of Mars's most peculiar clouds displays even more unusual characteristics than previously understood. Advanced meteorological modeling is unveiling new insights into Martian atmospheric phenomena.

articles.title: Science begins for Smile
articles.description: On 23 September, the European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready to start revealing how Earth responds to the wind of charged particles from the Sun. This follows a busy in-space commissioning period since the spacecraft launched on 19 May and reached its target orbit for science operations on 20 June.
articles.summary: The European-Chinese Smile mission has been declared operational and is beginning its groundbreaking study of Earth's magnetospheric response to solar wind. This collaborative mission opens new avenues for understanding planetary magnetism.

articles.title: Successful Earth flyby improves Juice’s course to Jupiter
articles.description: The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) skimmed the very outer edge of Earth’s atmosphere on 28 September, using the gravity of our home planet to alter its route to Jupiter using very little fuel.
articles.summary: The European Space Agency's Juice spacecraft successfully executed a precise Earth flyby to optimize its trajectory toward Jupiter. This gravitational assist maneuver sets the stage for groundbreaking exploration of Jupiter's icy moons.
